newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia lawyers group say political killing down.
newsitem.headline: Colombia lawyers group say political killing down.

text.p: Political murders in Colombia fell about 14 percent last year, according to a report released on Wednesday by a prominent lawyers' group.

But right-wing death squads, which the Colombian Commission of Jurists said were linked to the military, increased their activities, killing hundreds and creating thousands more refugees in 1996 than the previous year, the report said.

"The countryside has been bloodied," said Gustavo Gallon, director of the commission, during a press confrence to present the group's annual study of human rights violations in this trouble-torn Andean nation.
"Particularly worrisome are the continuing attacks on civilians and human rights workers," he added.

The report, "Colombia, human rights and humanitarian law: 1996," said 3,173 Colombians were murdered for political or ideological reasons last year. The lawyers' group reported 3,698 politically motivated killings in 1995.

The commission said right-wing paramilitary organisations, which are fighting for control of the Colombian countryside with Colombia's leftist rebels, were responsible for about 34 percent more killings last year than in 1995.
"Far from decidedly confronting the paramilitary groups, the government has facilitated their expansion," the report said.
Interior Minister Carlos Holmes, who also spoke during the conference, rejected the commission's conclusions about government involvement with right-wing groups.
"The data about human rights violations with respect to the state has nothing to do with reality," Holmes said.
The report also said threats from right-wing groups were a major reason why about 180,000 Colombians fled their homes last year -- 50,000 more than in 1995

Meanwhile, left-wing rebels -- who have battled the government for more than three decades -- were responsible for nearly 600 kidnappings last year, and have laced the Colombian countryside with landmines, the study said.

Colombia is the site of Latin America's longest running armed conflict, and has a murder rate eight times that of the United States. Police estimate the majority of the country's more than 26,000 annual murders are the result of common crime.
